options.text: Anything that can be seen with your eyes
Anything that has mass and takes up space
Only solids and liquids, because gases are empty space
Anything that sinks in water

items.explanation: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space (volume). That includes gases like air - a filled balloon has more mass than an empty one and takes up more space. The most common states of matter are solid, liquid, and gas.

items.stem: A scientist needs to measure the mass of a mineral sample and the volume of a liquid. Which tools and units should she use?

options.text: A ruler for mass in cm³, and a balance for volume in grams
A graduated cylinder for both, in milliliters
A triple beam balance for mass in grams, and a graduated cylinder for volume in milliliters
A triple beam balance for both, in grams

items.explanation: Mass is measured in grams (g) with a triple beam balance. Liquid volume is measured in milliliters (mL) with a graduated cylinder. A ruler measures the volume of regular solids in cm³ using V = length × width × height.

items.stem: A block is 3 cm long, 2 cm wide, and 2 cm tall. What is its volume?

options.text: 7 cm³, because 3 + 2 + 2 = 7
12 cm³, because 3 × 2 × 2 = 12
6 cm³, because 3 × 2 = 6
12 mL, because rulers measure in milliliters

items.explanation: Volume of a rectangular block = length × width × height = 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 cm³. You multiply the dimensions (not add them), and a ruler measurement gives cubic centimeters, not milliliters.

items.stem: An object has a mass of 24 g and a volume of 12 cm³. What is its density, and would it sink or float in water (1 g/cm³)?

options.text: 2 g/cm³ - it would sink, because its density is greater than water's
0.5 g/cm³ - it would float, because its density is less than water's
288 g/cm³ - it would sink, because mass times volume is huge
12 g/cm³ - it would sink, because volume equals density

items.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume = 24 ÷ 12 = 2 g/cm³. Since 2 g/cm³ is greater than water's density of 1 g/cm³, the object sinks. Density is a ratio - you divide, never multiply.

items.stem: Two balls are exactly the same size. Ball A is solid steel and Ball B is hollow plastic. Why is Ball A so much harder to lift?

options.text: Ball A has a bigger volume, so it weighs more
Ball A has more matter packed into the same space - a higher density and a greater mass
Ball B has more density spread across less mass
Same-size objects always have the same mass, so something else must explain it

items.explanation: The balls have equal volume, but the steel ball contains far more matter, giving it more mass and a much higher density - more matter packed into the same space. That's exactly the bowling ball vs. beach ball mystery from the start of the lesson.

items.stem: A balloon is weighed empty, then weighed again after being filled with air. The filled balloon has more mass. What does this show?

options.text: Air has volume but no mass at all
The balloon rubber got heavier as it stretched
Mass was created by the act of blowing it up
Air is matter, because it has mass and takes up space

items.explanation: Air is matter. The filled balloon has more mass because the air inside it has mass, and the air also takes up space (volume). Anything with mass and volume is matter, including gases.

options.text: The total weight of an object sitting on a balance
The amount of space an object takes up
How much matter is packed into a given amount of space
Whether an object is a solid, a liquid, or a gas

items.explanation: Density is how much matter (mass) is packed into a given volume: D = m ÷ V. It is not the same as mass alone or volume alone - it is the ratio of the two.

items.stem: A solid object is dropped into water and floats. What must be true about it?

options.text: Its mass is less than the mass of all the water
Its volume is smaller than the container holding the water
It has to be hollow somewhere inside
Its density is less than the density of water

items.explanation: Floating and sinking depend on density, not mass alone. An object floats when its density is less than the density of water (1 g/cm³). A huge steel ship floats because its overall density is low.

items.stem: How would you best measure the volume of a small, irregularly shaped rock?

options.text: Lower it into a graduated cylinder of water and measure how much the water rises
Multiply its length, width, and height with a ruler
Place it on a triple beam balance and read the grams
Estimate it by eye, since irregular shapes cannot be measured

items.explanation: An irregular solid has no neat dimensions to multiply, so use water displacement: the rise in water level in a graduated cylinder equals the rock's volume. A balance measures mass, not volume.

items.stem: Two objects have the same mass, but Object X has a much larger volume than Object Y. Which one has the greater density?

options.text: Object X, because it is bigger overall
They have equal density because their masses match
Object Y, because the same mass is squeezed into a smaller volume
Neither - density can only be compared when the masses differ

items.explanation: Density is mass ÷ volume. With equal mass, the object with the smaller volume (Object Y) packs that mass into less space, so it has the greater density.
